surveyDefinition.title: Smartwatches — consumer survey (China)
surveyDefinition.studyPurpose: Identify which of 4 behavioural segments each respondent belongs to, based on smartwatch usage intensity, purchase drivers, feature priorities, and upgrade/switching behaviour.

segments.name: Health-Committed Users
segments.description: Wear their smartwatch almost daily, primarily for continuous health and fitness tracking (heart rate, sleep, SpO2). They are willing to pay more for advanced sensors and accuracy, and are frustrated by inaccuracies and subscription fees for health metrics.

segments.name: Connectivity-Driven Users
segments.description: Use the smartwatch as an extension of their smartphone — for notifications, calls, and quick interactions. They value seamless ecosystem integration and app experience over fitness depth, and may not use all health features.

segments.name: Lifestyle-Style Owners
segments.description: Own a smartwatch as a fashion statement or status symbol, often choosing premium designs and brands. They use basic features (steps, time) but are less engaged with deep health tracking. They are attracted by design, brand reputation, and customization.

segments.name: Price-Sensitive Buyers
segments.description: Own a smartwatch but are highly conscious of price and value. They seek essential features at the lowest possible cost, are reluctant to pay for subscriptions, and may delay upgrades or choose older models. They are prone to switching if a better deal appears.

surveyDefinition.whatThisSurveyIs: A segmentation study of Smartwatches buyers in China. It asks how people use Smartwatches, how they choose it, and what would make them switch — then sorts respondents into the behavioural groups defined below. Questions stay at category level: no named brands, and nothing about adjacent categories.
surveyDefinition.whoseContextThisIs: Adults in China who buy or use Smartwatches for personal or household use. Respondents qualify if they: Individuals who currently own or have purchased a smartwatch in the past 12 months; Individuals who are actively considering purchasing a smartwatch within the next 6 months; Adults aged 18+ who make their own purchase decisions. Excluded: Businesses or institutions purchasing smartwatches in bulk for employees; Children under 18 (unless the study specifically targets kids' smartwatches, which is not the primary market); Individuals who only use basic fitness bands without smart features.
surveyDefinition.whyTheseRespondents: Consumers buy smartwatches for personal use, pay for them out of pocket, and decide on the model and brand themselves. While some businesses may purchase smartwatches for employees, the dominant and defining purchase is by individual consumers, making this a pure B2C market.
respondentBehaviours: Health and fitness tracking (steps, heart rate, sleep)
Smartphone integration for notifications and calls
Brand loyalty to smartphone ecosystems (Apple, Samsung, etc.)
whatIsDeliberatelyNotAsked: Age or household income as behavioural questions — no finding in this survey is driven by them. They are asked once, at the end, in Profiling, and used only to cross-tabulate the behavioural results.
Brand, company or manufacturer names — the survey stays at category level so findings are not tied to one competitor set.
Where the respondent lives — region is chosen when viewing the results, so asking it again would waste a question.
surveyDefinition.howToReadTheNumbers: Percentages are modelled estimates built from published market evidence — they are not measurements from fielded interviews, and should be read as an expected shape of response rather than a result. Single-choice, ranking and rating-scale questions sum to 100%. Multi-select questions do not — each option is an independent share of respondents choosing it. The N shown on each question is the display base for that item.

structure.storyline: Questions run in a planned narrative order: broad and easy first, specific and sensitive last.
structure.storylineSummary: The survey opens by establishing who owns a smartwatch and how they use it day-to-day, distinguishing health-focused users from connectivity-driven and style-led owners. It then traces the purchase journey — what triggered the buy, where they researched and bought, and what factors decided the choice. Next, it probes feature priorities, quality signals, and trade-offs, revealing what they value most and what they would sacrifice. Finally, it measures satisfaction, pain points, and future intent, identifying who is at risk of switching and what would retain them. The arc moves from broad usage…

targetCustomer.summary: Adult consumers of Smartwatches in China — who Individuals who currently own or have purchased a smartwatch in the past 12 months; Individuals who are actively considering purchasing a smartwatch within the next 6 months; Adults aged 18+ who make their own purchase decisions. The audience is defined as individual consumers who buy smartwatches for personal use, as they are the primary purchasers and decision-makers. The demographic and behavioral criteria capture both current owners and potential buyers to support a broad consumer survey.

metadata.studyPurpose: Identify which of 4 behavioural segments each respondent belongs to, based on smartwatch usage intensity, purchase drivers, feature priorities, and upgrade/switching behaviour.
metadata.segmentation_lens: Combination of usage/behavioural and jobs-to-be-done: the smartwatch category is split between those who use it as a fitness/health tool, those who use it as a connectivity extension, and those who use it as a lifestyle/status accessory — frequency alone would not separate these distinct purchase mo

segments.name: Health-Committed Users
segments.description: Wear their smartwatch almost daily, primarily for continuous health and fitness tracking (heart rate, sleep, SpO2). They are willing to pay more for advanced sensors and accuracy, and are frustrated by inaccuracies and subscription fees for health metrics.
segments.hypothesis: This group will report high usage frequency, prioritize health features over style, and show high interest in advanced health monitoring (blood pressure, sleep stages) even at a premium price.

segments.name: Connectivity-Driven Users
segments.description: Use the smartwatch as an extension of their smartphone — for notifications, calls, and quick interactions. They value seamless ecosystem integration and app experience over fitness depth, and may not use all health features.
segments.hypothesis: This group will show moderate usage frequency, prioritize brand ecosystem compatibility and notification reliability, and be less willing to pay for advanced health sensors they won't use.

segments.name: Lifestyle-Style Owners
segments.description: Own a smartwatch as a fashion statement or status symbol, often choosing premium designs and brands. They use basic features (steps, time) but are less engaged with deep health tracking. They are attracted by design, brand reputation, and customization.
segments.hypothesis: This group will show lower usage of health features, prioritize design and brand over functionality, and be willing to pay a premium for aesthetics and brand cachet.

segments.name: Price-Sensitive Buyers
segments.description: Own a smartwatch but are highly conscious of price and value. They seek essential features at the lowest possible cost, are reluctant to pay for subscriptions, and may delay upgrades or choose older models. They are prone to switching if a better deal appears.
segments.hypothesis: This group will report lower spend, prioritize price and battery life over advanced features, and show high sensitivity to subscription fees and promotional offers.

segmentModel.tie_break: The question 'bb1' (What made you decide to buy your current smartwatch?) is the most direct behavioural self-report because it captures the primary purchase motivation that cleanly separates the four segments: health tracking, phone integration, style, or price.
notes: Only options that clearly discriminate were scored; many neutral options were left unscored.

Some options (e.g., subscription fees) point to both health_committed_users and price_sensitive_buyers because both segments are frustrated by fees, but for different reasons: health users want the metrics, price-sensitive users don't want to pay.
Each segment has at least two scoring options and at least one 3-point option.
11 scoring weight(s) removed: they scored questions that were dropped as duplicates before publication.
segmentModel.excluded: Screening and Profiling questions are excluded from scoring: screeners carry no signal (everyone passed) and demographics are for cross-tabs, not segmentation.

fieldingNotes.recommendedSample: n=800-1,200 for stable segment-level sub-groups (roughly n>=312 per segment after weighting). At n=1,000 the margin of error on a whole-sample percentage is about ±3.1pp at 95% confidence; on a segment of n=200 it widens to about ±6.9pp, so segment-level differences under ~10pp should not be reported as real.
fieldingNotes.quotaControls: Apply quotas on the category-usage and frequency screeners so heavy users — who are more willing survey-takers — are not over-sampled.
scriptingNotes: Rotate the order of answer options on every non-ordinal question to remove primacy bias. Do NOT rotate ordinal scales (frequency bands, price bands, satisfaction) — their order carries meaning.
Anchor 'Other', 'None of these' and 'Prefer not to say' to the bottom of the list, exempt from rotation.
Every 'Other' option takes an open-text capture, coded back into the frame at analysis if any single verbatim exceeds 3%.
No routing or skip logic: every respondent sees every question, so the base is constant across the instrument.
Include one attention check in the middle third — a standard instructed-response item. Terminate on failure and replace.
Randomise the order of the two ranking/trade-off items between respondents so neither is systematically answered while fresher.
caveats: Percentages in this document are modelled from published market evidence, not measured from fielded interviews. Replace them with primary data once the study is run.
Ranking items are shown as a lighter-weight ranking exercise; run them as MaxDiff if you need more precision on driver importance.
Profiling questions are for cross-tabs only and are excluded from the segmentation scoring model.

metadata.storyline_summary: The survey opens by establishing who owns a smartwatch and how they use it day-to-day, distinguishing health-focused users from connectivity-driven and style-led owners. It then traces the purchase journey — what triggered the buy, where they researched and bought, and what factors decided the choice. Next, it probes feature priorities, quality signals, and trade-offs, revealing what they value most and what they would sacrifice. Finally, it measures satisfaction, pain points, and future intent, identifying who is at risk of switching and what would retain them. The arc moves from broad usage…
storyline_notes: Adapted the canonical arc to a durable wearable: replaced 'purchase frequency/restock' with 'purchase trigger' and 'research/discovery' to reflect the considered, infrequent nature of smartwatch buying.
Added a dedicated 'battery and charging' beat in preferences_expectations because battery life is a top pain point in the region and a key differentiator.
Included 'health tracking habits' in consumer_profile to separate health-committed users from others, as this is the primary job-to-be-done for many buyers.
In buying_behavior, emphasized research and discovery to reflect the region's mobile-first, online-review-driven shopping behaviour.
In satisfaction_future_intent, combined switching and future intent to capture both the risk of churn and the upgrade opportunity, as smartwatch owners often upgrade within the same ecosystem.
All beats are designed to be answered with closed questions and avoid asking age, income, or geography directly, in line with the segmentation rules.
metadata.classification_reason: Consumers buy smartwatches for personal use, pay for them out of pocket, and decide on the model and brand themselves. While some businesses may purchase smartwatches for employees, the dominant and defining purchase is by individual consumers, making this a pure B2C market.
